patient.name: Walter Grunsky
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe shortness of breath, worsening despite home nebulizer treatments

history.hpi: Wife called 911 after patient's breathing worsened over several hours despite using his home nebulizer twice. On EMS arrival he is tripoding, using accessory muscles, and speaking only 1-2 words at a time. He has a known history of end-stage COPD with two prior ICU admissions and one prior intubation. Wife reports he seemed 'more confused than usual' in the last 15 minutes.
pastMedical: Prior ICU admission x2 for COPD exacerbation
40 pack-year smoking history, quit 2 years ago
history.lastOralIntake: Sips of water this morning, no solid food
history.events: Progressive dyspnea over several hours, worsened despite two home nebulizer treatments; wife called 911 when he became difficult to arouse

scene.location: Single-story home, patient seated in recliner in living room, home O2 concentrator running nearby
scene.safety: No hazards to crew; home oxygen concentrator in use, no open flame nearby
scene.bystanders: Wife present, states he has been getting worse over the last several hours and is now harder to wake up
visualCues: Patient tripoding in recliner, visible accessory muscle use and intercostal retractions
Home nebulizer mask on floor next to chair
Home oxygen concentrator tubing connected to nasal cannula at 2L
Multiple inhalers and a hospital discharge folder on end table

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 69-year-old male with known end-stage COPD in severe respiratory distress, tripoding with accessory muscle use, speaking only 1-2 words at a time. He is increasingly difficult to arouse per his wife.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but severely labored, audible expiratory wheeze
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Severe accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, prolonged expiratory phase, speaking 1-2 words per breath
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, bounding, skin diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Follows simple commands slowly, intact strength in all extremities
otherFindings: Diffuse expiratory wheezing, diminished breath sounds at bases
Barrel chest, use of sternocleidomastoid muscles
Wife reports increasing difficulty arousing him over last 15 minutes

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes severe respiratory distress with impending failure and initiates CPAP with nebulized bronchodilator administered in-line, coaching the patient through mask application.

phases.name: CPAP with in-line duoneb started
phases.description: CPAP is applied with albuterol/ipratropium nebulized in-line through a T-connector. The patient initially tolerates the mask with coaching, and permissive hypoxia (SpO2 goal ≥90%, higher COPD tolerance) is accepted rather than chasing a normal saturation.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing severe respiratory distress with an elevated EtCO2 and diminishing mental status, the crew initiates non-invasive ventilation early per protocol, with nebulized bronchodilator delivered in-line through a CPAP-compatible T-connector.

clinicalPresentation.airway: CPAP mask sealed, tolerating with coaching
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Still labored but slightly less retractions, RR 28
otherFindings: Wife coached to help maintain reassurance

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate CPAP with in-line nebulized bronchodilator; coach patient through mask seal
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be considered early for severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure. NIV options include continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP)... Nebulized medications may be administered through a CPAP or BiPAP mask. A specialized T-connector with a spring valve assembly is required to allow maintenance of positive airway pressure.
expectedActions.rationale: Early NIV with bronchodilator is the first-line escalation for severe COPD-related bronchospasm and impending failure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Accept SpO2 ≥90% rather than titrating to normal saturation; monitor EtCO2 trend, not absolute normalization
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Permissive hypoxia (SPO2 ≥ 90%) may be appropriate in patients with COPD or other complex respiratory pathology... Patients who have end stage COPD may have chronically elevated EtCO2 as high as 50s–60s, and thus tolerate elevated EtCO2 better so normalization may not be a good target.
expectedActions.rationale: Chasing a normal SpO2/EtCO2 in a chronic CO2-retainer can worsen outcomes; the trend matters more than the absolute number.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain continuous waveform capnography and pulse oximetry throughout NIV trial
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with significant respiratory distress should have continuous pulse oximetry and waveform capnography monitoring for both assessment and for guiding therapy.
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous capnography is the earliest objective sign of CPAP failure and progressing CO2 narcosis.

transitions.condition: Despite a well-sealed CPAP trial with bronchodilator, the patient's EtCO2 continues climbing and mental status worsens; crew recognizes CPAP failure per protocol and removes CPAP to proceed with RSI.

transitions.if: CPAP continued despite worsening mental status
transitions.condition: Crew continues CPAP without reassessing for failure criteria despite objective signs of deterioration (rising EtCO2, worsening mental status), delaying necessary escalation to airway management.

phases.name: CPAP failure recognized, RSI performed
phases.description: The patient's EtCO2 continues to rise and mental status deteriorates despite an adequate CPAP trial, meeting CPAP-failure criteria. The crew removes CPAP, preoxygenates, and proceeds with RSI, selecting ketamine for its bronchodilatory properties given the underlying severe bronchospasm.
phases.triggerCondition: After a full CPAP trial with in-line bronchodilator fails to reverse the trend — EtCO2 continues rising and mental status worsens toward unresponsiveness — the crew recognizes CPAP failure per protocol, discontinues CPAP, and proceeds directly to RSI rather than continuing a failing non-invasive strategy.

clinicalPresentation.airway: CPAP removed, BVM-assisted with OPA in place during RSI setup
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Shallow, minimal air movement, RR 10 and irregular
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, skin diaphoretic and cool
otherFindings: CPAP removed after failure criteria met
EtCO2 rising further despite treatment, consistent with CO2 narcosis
Two experienced airway practitioners at bedside for RSI

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize CPAP failure (worsened mental status, rising EtCO2); remove CPAP and escalate
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If patient deteriorates on CPAP/BiPAP (e.g., worsened mental status, increasing EtCO2, vomiting), remove CPAP/BiPAP and escalate airway management options as above.
expectedActions.rationale: Recognizing CPAP failure promptly prevents progression to respiratory arrest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2 and positive pressure ventilation for at least 2 minutes before RSI
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient should be pre-oxygenated with high flow oxygen, and positive pressure ventilation for a minimum of two minutes prior to the procedure.
expectedActions.rationale: Adequate preoxygenation reduces the risk of peri-intubation hypoxia and hypoxic cardiac arrest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Fentanyl 78 mcg IV push (78 kg × 1 mcg/kg) 2-3 minutes prior to intubation attempt
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider pre-medication with Fentanyl, 1 mcg/kg, 2-3 minutes prior to intubation attempt.
expectedActions.rationale: Blunts the sympathetic/hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ketamine 117 mg IV push (78 kg × 1.5 mg/kg) as induction agent
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer induction sedative agent: Etomidate IV push, 0.2-0.3 mg/kg OR Ketamine IV push, 1-2 mg/kg OR Midazolam IV push, 0.05-0.10 mg/kg.
expectedActions.rationale: Ketamine provides bronchodilation in addition to sedation, favorable in a patient with severe bronchospasm.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rocuronium 78 mg IV push (78 kg × 1 mg/kg) as paralytic
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer paralytic agent: Succinylcholine IV push, 1-2 mg/kg OR Rocuronium IV push, 1 mg/kg OR Vecuronium IV push, 0.1 mg/kg.
expectedActions.rationale: Provides complete paralysis to optimize first-pass intubation success.

transitions.if: Tube confirmed, ventilated for permissive hypercapnia
transitions.condition: Endotracheal tube placement is confirmed with waveform capnography and bilateral breath sounds; patient is secured and mechanically ventilated with a target EtCO2 appropriate for a chronic CO2 retainer rather than normalization.

phases.name: Tube confirmed, ventilated for permissive hypercapnia
phases.description: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography and secured. Ventilation is titrated to gradually decrease the patient's chronically elevated EtCO2 rather than aggressively normalizing it, avoiding the hemodynamic and cerebral perfusion risks of rapid correction.
phases.triggerCondition: After successful RSI and tube placement, capnography confirms correct position; the crew secures the tube and titrates ventilation to a gradual EtCO2 reduction appropriate for a chronic hypercapnic patient.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Secured with endotracheal tube, confirmed placement
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mechanically ventilated, 10-12 breaths/min, 6-8 mL/kg tidal volume
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, skin warming slightly
otherFindings: ETT secured at appropriate depth, confirmed with continuous waveform capnography
Bilateral breath sounds present, no gastric sounds

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm tube placement with waveform capnography, bilateral breath sounds, absent gastric sounds
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Confirm placement of advanced airway (endotracheal tube, SGA) with waveform capnography (most reliable), absent gastric sounds, and bilateral breath sounds.
expectedActions.rationale: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation method and must be used before trusting tube placement.

expectedActions.shortAction: Titrate ventilation to gradually decrease EtCO2 rather than rapid normalization
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: to gradually decrease EtCO2 in chronically and acutely severely hypercarbic patients including post-arrest.
expectedActions.rationale: Rapid correction of chronic hypercapnia can precipitate dangerous alkalosis and hemodynamic instability.

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide post-intubation sedation with fentanyl and midazolam or ketamine per protocol
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Intubated patients should be provided appropriate sedation with sedative or opioid medications, and sedation titrated to an appropriate target level using RASS score or similar scale.
expectedActions.rationale: Adequate sedation prevents patient-ventilator dyssynchrony and reduces physiologic stress response.

phases.name: CPAP continued despite worsening mental status
phases.description: The crew continues CPAP without reassessing for failure, despite the patient's mental status continuing to decline and EtCO2 continuing to climb. The patient progresses toward respiratory arrest as CO2 narcosis worsens under the mask.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew does not reassess for CPAP failure criteria despite objective signs (rising EtCO2, worsening mental status) and continues the mask trial, allowing CO2 narcosis to progress toward respiratory arrest.

clinicalPresentation.airway: CPAP mask still in place, minimal spontaneous effort visible
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Agonal, RR 6, minimal chest rise under the mask
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: No purposeful movement, minimal response to pain
otherFindings: CPAP mask never removed despite worsening mental status
EtCO2 continues climbing under the mask

expectedActions.shortAction: Remove CPAP immediately, begin BVM ventilation, prepare emergent RSI
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If patient deteriorates on CPAP/BiPAP (e.g., worsened mental status, increasing EtCO2, vomiting), remove CPAP/BiPAP and escalate airway management options as above.
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition of CPAP failure has allowed progression to near-respiratory-arrest; immediate rescue ventilation is required before RSI can even be safely attempted.
